segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening the Case

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' most ambitious novel apart, carefully, to see how it works and why it still matters.

I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be moving through this extraordinary book — its fog and its fire, its comedy and its fury, its twin narrative voices and its vast, interconnected cast.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the opening that may be the most famous in all of Victorian fiction.
Three extraordinary people have joined me for this journey, and I want to introduce them properly — because each brings something the novel itself seems to require.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a clock — with deep affection for how the mechanism works.
She is precisely the person you want when a single sentence is doing six things at once — which in Bleak House happens on virtually every page.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian of the Victorian period, which means he can tell us what the Court of Chancery actually was — not just as metaphor, but as lived institutional nightmare.
He brings a controlled fury to Dickens' satire that I find genuinely illuminating — and occasionally alarming, in the best way.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since — which tells you everything about the kind of reader she is.
She reads with her whole self — emotionally, intellectually, and with wonderful attentiveness to the music of Dickens' prose.
Eleanor, James, Caroline — welcome, all three of you.
Let's start where Dickens starts — in the fog.
The opening of Bleak House is one of those rare cases where you can feel a novelist solving a problem in real time — on the page, in front of you.
The problem is: how do you open a novel about an institution so vast and so suffocating that it has consumed years, fortunes, and entire families?
Dickens' answer is atmospheric annihilation.
He doesn't introduce a character, or a scene, or even a plot.
He introduces a condition — fog — and then lets it eat everything.
He writes — and I find this almost unbearably good —
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That repetition — "fog up," "fog down" — it's not descriptive writing, it's incantatory writing.
Dickens is performing the fog, not just reporting it.
And then — this is the genius of it — the fog closes in on the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall.
The natural world and the legal world turn out to be the same fog.
What Eleanor is identifying as a structural and poetic achievement is also a piece of ruthlessly accurate social observation.
The Court of Chancery, by 1852, was a system so tangled in its own procedures that cases had genuinely been running for decades without resolution.
The case of Jennens v. Jennens — which Dickens drew on for Jarndyce and Jarndyce — had been in Chancery for over a century.
So when Dickens writes about fog, he is choosing the precise metaphor — one that obscures, disorients, and kills by slow suffocation.
He gives us the Lord Chancellor surrounded by fog, and then he tells us —

"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition which this High Court of Chancery, most pestilent of hoary sinners, holds this day in the sight of heaven and earth."
"Most pestilent of hoary sinners" — applied to a court of law, in the opening pages of a novel.
That is not a metaphor cautiously introduced — that is a declaration of war.
And he was right to be angry.
What stays with me, reading that opening — and I've read it now more times than I can honestly count — is how much grief is already encoded in it.
Before we've met a single person, before we know anything about Esther or Richard or Ada, we already feel the weight of what this world does to people.
And then Dickens introduces the suitors — the people caught in Jarndyce and Jarndyce — with this extraordinary tenderness.
He calls them, in that first chapter, "the man from Shropshire" — this nameless, ruined figure haunting the court.
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good that has ever come of it."
And that line — that bleak, devastating joke — it's Dickens telling you exactly what kind of novel this is going to be.
The comedy and the cruelty are inseparable.
They always are, in Dickens — but never more so than here.
Caroline's point about tenderness is exactly right — and it connects to something technically fascinating about this opening, which is its narrative position.
The first chapter is in the third person — this sweeping, omniscient, almost wrathful voice that describes the fog and Chancery.
But then — in Chapter Three — a completely different narrator walks in.
Esther Summerson, self-deprecating, warm, specific, unreliable in the most interesting ways.
Esther opens with — and this is among my favourite opening lines in any Victorian novel —
"I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages, for I know I am not clever."
Of course she is devastatingly clever — and Dickens knows that we know it.
The gap between what Esther says about herself and what we observe her doing — that gap is where so much of the novel's emotional meaning lives.
The dual narration also has a specific social logic that I think is worth naming.
The third-person narrator sees everything from above — institutions, systems, the sweep of historical injustice.
Esther sees everything from below — from inside the human costs of those systems.
She is an illegitimate woman with no legal standing, no inheritance, no place in the world that the law recognises.
And Dickens gives this woman — this precise social nobody — one of the two controlling narrative voices of his longest and most complex novel.
That is a structural argument, not merely a stylistic one.
And I think readers feel that argument even when they can't name it — which is why Esther tends to inspire such fierce loyalty.
Some readers find her exasperating — too modest, too self-effacing.
But on re-reading, what you see is a woman who has been told, from childhood, that her existence is a shame — and who nonetheless shows up, every single day, with extraordinary competence and love.
Her godmother tells her, brutally, as a child —
"Your mother, Esther, is your disgrace, and you were hers."
That is the sentence that makes Esther who she is.
Everything she becomes — every act of generosity, every denial of her own needs — comes from having been told that her very birth was a crime.
She deserves better. She always has.
We are barely past the opening chapters and already — fog, fury, a court that consumes lives, and a narrator who has been told she has no right to exist.
Dickens is not easing us in gently.
In our next segment, we'll move deeper into Chancery itself — what it meant to be caught inside Jarndyce and Jarndyce, and why Dickens chose a lawsuit as the engine of an entire world.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Wards of Court: Richard\'s Slow Unraveling

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes its time with one of the great long novels of the Victorian age.
Today's segment is one I've been looking forward to — and dreading — in equal measure.
We're turning our full attention to Richard Carstone: ward of the court of Chancery, and one of Dickens' most quietly devastating creations.
Eleanor Hartley is here to examine how Dickens engineers Richard's decline — the sentence-level choices, the structural ironies.
James Blackstone will place Jarndyce versus Jarndyce in its real historical context — what such a suit actually meant to those trapped inside it.
And Caroline Woodcourt will bring the reader's experience: what it feels like to watch someone you've come to love walk steadily toward ruin.
Let's begin with the man himself — or the boy, really, because that's how we first encounter him.
What strikes me every time I return to Richard's opening chapters is how thoroughly Dickens flatters us into liking him.
He arrives at Bleak House with Ada Clare, and the two of them are so luminously young, so genuinely appealing, that we're almost seduced alongside Esther.
Dickens gives Richard wit, charm, physical energy — all the signals we read as promise.
And then — very quietly, in almost throwaway asides — he plants the seeds of what will destroy him.
There's that crucial early moment when Richard can't settle on a profession — law, medicine, the army — and he flits between them with almost comic speed.
Esther and Jarndyce see it clearly as a warning sign.
But Dickens has written Richard's restlessness with such infectious energy that the reader keeps giving him the benefit of the doubt.
That gap between what we see and what we allow ourselves to believe — that's the trap Dickens sets for the reader.
And I think you need that seduction, Eleanor, because otherwise the Chancery machinery looks too nakedly brutal from the outset.
What Dickens understood — and what I find remarkable given the limits of public knowledge at the time — is how the real court of Chancery operated as a slow-consumption machine.
Cases in Chancery in the 1840s and 1850s could run for literally decades, accumulating costs that swallowed estates whole.
The heirs of the original litigants would inherit the suits along with the debts.
Richard isn't simply a young man making bad choices — he's a young man who has inherited a pathological relationship with hope itself.
The suit tells him, constantly, that there is a fortune just over the horizon, that patience and vigilance will be rewarded.

Jarndyce puts it with characteristic terseness when he warns Richard — something to the effect that no one who pins his faith to the suit ever profits from it, that it has a corrupting gravity all its own.
'Suffer no fancy to lead you to connect the suit with any hope of good to yourselves.'
Jarndyce says this early and repeatedly — and Richard cannot hear it, because the suit has already rewritten the frequencies on which he receives information.
What breaks my heart is precisely that Richard is not stupid.
He's perceptive, generous, capable of genuine insight — there are moments when he almost sees himself clearly.
When he's in the army, he writes with real lucidity about how the suit has been pulling at him.
But then the next letter reveals that he's sold his commission, is back in London, and is throwing himself into the case again.
Reading those letters as they arrive in Esther's narrative, you feel the lurch — the hope, then the sinking.
Dickens gives us a very precise account of what addiction looks like from the outside — in someone you love.
He describes Richard, by the later chapters, as having lost weight, as moving with a kind of febrile urgency that frightens everyone around him.
'He has flushed and feverish look of one who has been long haunted by an uneasy conscience.'
That word 'haunted' — it's doing such work there.
Richard is haunted not by guilt exactly, but by the phantom of a future that will never arrive.
And I want to press on the structural decision Dickens makes with the dual narration here, because it's crucial.
We see Richard primarily through Esther's eyes — and Esther loves him.
Her narration is scrupulously honest, but it's also filtered through affection and something very close to maternal protectiveness.
So we never quite see Richard through a cold eye — not the way we see, say, Skimpole.
The third-person narrator actually gets comparatively little Richard compared to Esther's chapters.
But when that narrator does brush up against him — briefly, in the Chancery scenes — the description is pitiless.
There's a late scene where we see Richard in court, and Dickens describes him watching the lawyers with the intensity of someone who has confused the map for the territory.
'He had his papers always with him, and had the greatest interest in all the proceedings.'
It sounds almost admirable in isolation — and that's the horror of it.
The vocabulary of diligence and engagement is applied to a man consuming himself alive.
That's exactly the ideological function the court served in reality, too.
Chancery was extraordinarily good at making its processes look like progress.
There were always new motions, new hearings, new opinions to be obtained — the apparatus was perpetually in motion, generating the sensation of activity without resolution.
And what Dickens correctly identifies is the particular cruelty of hope deferred over years — it doesn't merely disappoint; it corrupts the capacity to want anything else.
Richard cannot invest himself in medicine, or the law, or the army, not because he lacks ability, but because none of those things is Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
The suit has colonized his imagination.

There's a passage where Vholes — Richard's sinister solicitor — speaks with perfect professional calm about the progress of the case, and one is reminded of nothing so much as a physician describing a patient's decline as 'not without hope.'
Dickens describes Vholes as keeping 'a smooth, damp, cold hand' — a phrase of almost physical revulsion.
'A dull, forlorn, and miserable-looking man, always at work in a mysterious part of his office which no light ever touched.'
That detail — 'no light ever touched' — is Dickens telling you exactly what kind of work this is.
Vholes is one of those characters where Dickens refuses to let satire let you off the hook.
He's so obviously vampiric — the three daughters, the aged father in the Vale of Taunton — it should be comic.
But the way Vholes watches Richard — with that patient, proprietorial attention — it's genuinely nauseating.
What I find almost unbearable is Richard's defense of him — Richard insisting that Vholes is a good man, an honest man.
Because by that point, to doubt Vholes is to doubt the suit, and to doubt the suit is to lose the only structure that holds Richard's sense of self together.
There's that terrible scene, late in the novel, when Ada has secretly married Richard and Esther goes to visit them in their mean lodgings.
'He was not only worn and haggard, but he was much changed in his manner — at once more furtive and more fierce.'
'Furtive and fierce' — those two words placed next to each other feel almost clinical.
It's the portrait of a mind eating itself from the inside.
And crucially, Dickens does something very strange and brave with the ending.
When the suit finally collapses — when it's revealed that the entire estate has been consumed by legal costs — Richard is there in the courtroom.
And the moment that destroys him is not grief.
It's the collapse of narrative — the story he has been living inside simply ends, without resolution, without meaning.
Dickens writes it with remarkable compression — no melodrama, just the quick physical dissolution of a man whose organizing principle has been removed.
'The suit has lapsed and melted away,' he tells Esther — with a gentleness that is more devastating than any outburst could be.
'Call the next cause.'
That's the Chancery clerk, moving immediately on to the next case — and it's the most indifferent dismissal imaginable.
Richard Carstone's entire life, in three syllables, followed by a comma.
That moment has a real-world counterpart, and it still makes me angry.
There was in fact a case — Jennens v Jennens — which ran from around 1798 and was never conclusively settled, consuming a fortune estimated in the millions.
The heirs of claimants died waiting.
Dickens knew these cases — he had been a Chancery reporter himself as a young man — and he knew that the system's cruelty was not incidental but structural.
Richard is not a cautionary tale about imprudence — he is the system's natural product.
And what stays with me, long after the novel ends, is what's lost with Richard.
He dies — offstage, mercifully, in a way that feels almost like a kindness from Dickens — and Ada is left widowed, with their child.
But what I mourn is the Richard of the early chapters — the laughing boy on the steps of Bleak House, full of plans.
Esther puts it with a quiet precision that undoes me every time.
'He was young, and handsome, and had been full of promise.'
'Had been' — that past perfect.
It collapses a whole life into a tense.
That is a beautiful — and devastating — place to rest for a moment.
A life collapsed into a grammatical tense.
Richard Carstone — genial, brilliant, doomed — is Dickens' argument, in human form, against an institution that consumed people without mercy and without notice.
We'll be back shortly to consider the women who bear witness to his unraveling — and what it costs them.

segments.title: Crossing Class Lines: Jo and the Weight of Social Machinery

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast where we spend serious time with one of the great novels of the English language.
Today's segment takes us to one of the most devastating threads in the entire novel: Jo, the crossing-sweeper of Tom-all-Alone's.
Jo is, by any measure, Dickens' most unsparing portrait of what it means to exist at the absolute floor of Victorian society.
With me to unpack all of that are three people whose thinking I trust enormously on this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens with a craftsperson's eye — she sees the machinery behind the effects.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian who can tell us exactly what the Victorian institutions surrounding Jo actually were and how they worked.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has loved this novel since she was a teenager and brings the reader's lived experience of it.
Let's begin with first principles. Eleanor — what is Dickens actually doing when he introduces Jo?
Jo's introduction is one of the great rhetorical gambits in Victorian fiction, and I don't think people fully appreciate how constructed it is.
Dickens comes at the reader almost accusingly.
He sets up this devastating little catechism — what does Jo know? Almost nothing. What can Jo do? Almost nothing.
And then he delivers that extraordinary line about Jo being a dirty, ugly, disagreeable boy — and pivots immediately to ask us what we expect.
"Turn that dog's descendants loose, who are his parents, brothers, sisters? What chances or mischances have made him thus?"
The syntax enacts the argument. Those questions tumble out as if they've been suppressed and can no longer be held back.
Dickens is not sentimentalizing Jo — he's indicting the system that produced him, by making us look, really look, at what that system creates.
And the indictment is precise — which is what makes it so damning, as opposed to merely sentimental.
Jo exists in a specific legal and administrative void that Dickens understood better than most journalists of his day.
Under the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, relief was tied to the parish of settlement — and Jo has no parish, no settlement, no recorded existence whatsoever.
He is ordered to "move on" not as a metaphor — that is the actual language of the Vagrancy Acts.
Constables had statutory authority to move on anyone who could not demonstrate a fixed abode or lawful occupation.
So when Dickens writes that Jo is constantly being moved on, he is being technically accurate about a machinery of exclusion that was entirely real.
And what the novel captures — with extraordinary fidelity — is that this machinery has no malicious intent. It simply runs.
That phrase — "it simply runs" — is exactly what makes reading Jo's chapters so difficult. There's no villain to blame.
And I think what Dickens does with the "move on" refrain is something close to musical in its effect.
Each time it comes back, it has gathered more weight. By the time Jo is dying, that phrase has become almost unbearable.
There's a passage where the narrator addresses Jo directly — and the tenderness of it just stops me every time I reach it.

"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
Every repetition of "Dead" is a hammer blow. Dickens is not letting you mourn quietly and move on yourself.
He is holding your face to it.
That passage is technically an apostrophe — the narrator turning from the story to address the reader and the ruling class simultaneously.
And it's in the third-person narrator's voice, not Esther's. The switch matters enormously.
Esther could grieve for Jo personally — and she does. But this apostrophe requires the omniscient narrator's authority to work.
It has to come from a voice that can address "Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends" — a voice with the range to indict an entire society.
The dual narration is one of the novel's great structural inventions, and moments like Jo's death are precisely where it pays off.
The address to the "Wrong Reverends" is pointed in a way that would have stung contemporary readers, and was meant to.
Dickens was writing in the early 1850s, when the Sanitary Reform movement was at a critical juncture.

Edwin Chadwick's 1842 Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population had established that disease — including the smallpox Jo spreads — was fundamentally a product of poverty and neglect, not moral failing.
But the Established Church had largely resisted that framing, preferring to see destitution as a spiritual condition requiring moral instruction.
The "Wrong Reverends" is Dickens saying, in his most controlled fury: you had the diagnosis, you had the resources, and you chose doctrine over drainage.
"Doctrine over drainage" — I want that on a plaque somewhere.
But what I find so remarkable about Jo as a character — beyond the polemic — is how carefully observed he is as a consciousness.
He doesn't understand most of what happens to him. And Dickens renders that incomprehension with absolute fidelity, without condescension.
When Tulkinghorn and Inspector Bucket quiz Jo about the mysterious woman in the graveyard, there's this moment where Jo is trying so hard to tell the truth —
"I don't know nothink about no lady. I never see no lady."
The grammar is wrong, the syntax is broken — and yet the utterance is completely transparent in its honesty. Jo is incapable of guile.
He doesn't have enough language to lie. And that is its own kind of devastating indictment.
The dialect is doing extraordinary work there, and it's a decision that could have gone badly wrong.
Dickens' use of non-standard grammar in character speech is often read as comic — and sometimes it is.
But with Jo, the broken syntax is not comic. It registers as cognitive deprivation — not stupidity, but the absence of the tools of thought.
Compare how Jo speaks to how Harold Skimpole speaks — all elaborate, beautiful, self-exculpating sentences.
Skimpole has all the language in the world and uses it entirely to evade responsibility. Jo has almost none, and cannot evade anything.
That contrast is engineered. Dickens built it deliberately into the architecture of the novel.
The Skimpole contrast is worth pausing on, because Skimpole is explicitly coded as belonging to the educated, cultivated class.
And there is a moment — one of the novel's most quietly sickening moments — where Skimpole takes a bribe from Bucket to give up Jo's hiding place.
Half a sovereign. That is what Jo's safety is worth to Harold Skimpole.
And Skimpole, characteristically, wraps this transaction in the language of beautiful necessity — he tells himself he is simply being natural, childlike, free of worldly hypocrisy.
What Dickens is showing us is that refined language, cultural capital, all the markers of civilization — can coexist perfectly well with moral vacancy.
In fact, in Skimpole's case, they facilitate it.
And Esther's horror at the Skimpole revelation is one of the places where I think her narration is most trustworthy — most adult.
She has always been uncomfortable with Skimpole, even when she couldn't articulate why. And then she sees it clearly.
But the character who crosses the class line most literally — physically crosses it — in connection with Jo is Lady Dedlock.
She disguises herself as a servant to go with Jo to the pauper's graveyard where Nemo — her former lover — is buried.
And Jo, who is utterly without guile, senses something is wrong about her — wrong in the sense of too fine — but cannot name it.
He says her hands are different. Different from a servant's hands. He notices, and he cannot say more than that.
In that small observation is the whole weight of class distinction — perceived by the one person with no stake in maintaining it.
That detail about the hands is breathtaking, because it does exactly what only fiction can do — it makes an abstract social fact sensory.
Class is written on the body. That is the novel's argument, and Jo reads it on Lady Dedlock without any theoretical framework whatsoever.
He knows what he knows from looking at thousands of hands, because hands are what Jo encounters at the level of the crossing — coins dropped into his palm.
His entire epistemology comes from the street. And it is, in its own way, devastatingly accurate.
The graveyard scene is also doing documentary work that I think gets underappreciated.
Pauper burial grounds in 1850s London were a genuine public health scandal — overcrowded, poorly maintained, often directly contaminating the surrounding streets and water supply.
The Burial Acts weren't passed until 1852 and 1853 — Dickens was serializing Bleak House during that exact legislative window.
When Dickens describes that graveyard as a place where the waters of corruption seep outward into the surrounding slum, he is not being metaphorical.
He is describing a mechanism of infection that public health reformers had been documenting for a decade.

And Jo, carrying that infection outward — spreading smallpox first to Esther, then into the wider social world — is the novel's great emblem of how contagion crosses class lines whether the upper classes wish it or not.
And Esther's disfigurement — her scarring from the smallpox — is the novel making that metaphor literal on the body of its own narrator.
Esther is the one character who consistently sees Jo as a human being — who tends him, speaks to him with dignity.
And she pays for that compassion with her face. Dickens is ruthless about the cost of goodness.
There is a moment before Jo dies — he's with Woodcourt, the doctor — where Jo tries to say the Lord's Prayer.
"Jo, can you say what I say?" "I'll say anythink as you say, sir, for I knows it's good."
He can't reproduce the words. But the faith — the instinct toward something larger — is there. It's heartbreaking and it's not sentimental.
Because Jo dies not having been saved, not having been instructed, not having been given the tools that civilization could have given him and withheld.
What you've all been tracing is a network — Jo at the centre of it, touching every layer of this society and contaminating them, not through malice but through mere existence.
The machinery of class, as James put it, simply runs — and Jo is what gets caught in it.
We're going to take that thread forward and look at another set of institutions Dickens dismantles in this novel — the law itself, and the long shadow of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.

segments.title: Bleak House's Tangled Secrets: Lady Dedlock Exposed

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast where we take Dickens' great sprawling masterpiece apart — carefully, lovingly — and look at what's inside.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the novel's most gripping threads: the secret life of Lady Dedlock — and what happens when that secret begins to unravel.
Joining me are three people who know this novel with an intimacy that I find genuinely enviable.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed — and I mean that as a compliment — with the architecture of Dickens' sentences.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian who can tell you exactly what Chancery smelled like in 1852, and why that matters enormously.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devotee who has read Bleak House five times and still finds new things to stop and stare at.
The question before us today: who is Lady Dedlock, really — and how does Dickens build the slow, terrible revelation of her past?
What strikes me first about Lady Dedlock is the way Dickens introduces her — almost as a concept before she becomes a person.
She arrives in those early chapters defined entirely by her boredom — that famous, glacial ennui which is simultaneously her armour and her prison.
Dickens writes of her world, early in the novel, that it is
"as empty as the shell of a great spider who has been long dead."
That image is extraordinary — the spider's shell, not a web, not a creature, but an evacuated husk of something once predatory.
Dickens is telling us from the very start that this woman's outward life is a complete fiction — and the real creature has long since fled.
That's exactly right, and the fiction is one she's had to maintain with extraordinary discipline — because the alternative is social annihilation.
We have to understand what a baronet's wife in 1850s England stood to lose if an illegitimate child came to light.
We're not talking about social embarrassment — we're talking about the complete erasure of her position, her marriage, her legal standing.
Dickens understood this with absolute precision, which is why the moment she sees Captain Hawdon's handwriting on a legal document hits so hard.
Tulkinghorn is watching her face at that moment, and Dickens gives us the horror of that surveillance with chilling economy.
The lawyer already knows he holds a weapon before he has decided precisely how to use it.
What I've never gotten over — on any reading — is that first crack in the ice.
Lady Dedlock sees the handwriting, and she faints — or nearly faints — and Dickens writes it as if the entire architecture of her self has momentarily given way.
He says she is taken ill, and Tulkinghorn observes with that reptile stillness of his.
"My Lady Dedlock had been for many years, what, in the light of the present crisis, it was her pride to be — utterly unknown."
That phrase — utterly unknown — is devastating when you feel its full weight.
She has spent a lifetime cultivating the condition of being unreadable, and now one sheet of paper has made her visible.
And this is where the dual narration becomes so structurally brilliant, because we experience Lady Dedlock from two completely different angles.
In the third-person narrative — Dickens' own voice — she is seen from outside, theatrical, almost mythological.
But Esther, our first-person narrator, meets Lady Dedlock and feels something she can't quite name — a pull, an inexplicable recognition.
Esther says, and this is such a quietly extraordinary moment,
"I was rendered motionless. Not so much by her beauty, as by something in her face that I could not separate from my old remembrances."
The reader understands what Esther cannot consciously articulate — she is looking at her mother.
That dramatic irony is exquisitely managed — Dickens gives us the emotion before the information, which is exactly the right order.
I want to dwell on Tulkinghorn for a moment, because he's more than a villain — he is an institution.
He represents the way that legal and social power in Victorian England operated — not through open coercion but through the hoarding of information.
Dickens describes him as living among the mummies of buried secrets, surrounding himself with dark rooms full of locked boxes.
There's a passage where Dickens says of him,
"He is of what is called the old school — a phrase generally meaning any school that seems never to have been young."
That dry parenthetical is Dickens at his most politically pointed — the 'old school' as a system designed to perpetuate its own power, never reformed, never questioned.
And Tulkinghorn is its perfect embodiment — he doesn't want Lady Dedlock's secret for money, which would be comprehensible. He wants it because possession of it is power.
And against that implacable machinery, Lady Dedlock does the only thing she can — she tries to find her daughter.
The disguise sequence — where she borrows Jenny the brickmaker's wife's clothes to move unseen through London — is one of the novel's most viscerally moving passages.
A baronet's wife putting on a working woman's shawl and going out into the fog — Dickens doesn't explain the symbolism, he just lets it breathe.
And when she does finally encounter Esther — when she kneels before her, and Esther describes it — Dickens writes,
"I raised my mother up, praying and beseeching her not to stoop before me. I did so, in broken, incoherent, loving words."
Esther is the one who raises her. The child lifts the parent. That reversal carries everything.
That scene is where Dickens earns every slow chapter of build-up — the payoff is so precisely calibrated.
But what I find most technically audacious is how Dickens handles Lady Dedlock's final arc — her flight, and her death at the gate of the pauper's graveyard.
She dies at the very spot where Captain Hawdon — Nemo — is buried. The man whose name means 'no one' in Latin.
The geography of death in this novel is never accidental — it is always moral.
And Dickens gives us the discovery through Bucket and Esther, who have been chasing her through a London that is pure nightmare — fog, mud, frozen roads.
When Esther finds her lying at that gate, still dressed in the poor woman's clothes, Dickens writes with absolute quiet restraint.
"I saw before me, lying on the step, the mother of the dead child."
He doesn't say Lady Dedlock. He doesn't say my mother. He says 'the mother of the dead child.' It's annihilating.
And historically that death is not just tragic — it's a verdict.
She dies outside a pauper's graveyard — the most degraded resting place in Victorian London, the place for the nameless and the destitute.
The man she loved was buried there — among the very people that her class spent its entire existence ignoring.
Dickens is making a structural argument: love that crosses class lines is not punished by society alone — it is punished by the entire architecture of a system that makes such love invisible.
The graveyard where Jo is famously described earlier is the same graveyard. That's not coincidence — that's Dickens making everything connect.
And what Dickens refuses to do — which I think is his greatest act of mercy toward her — is let Lady Dedlock be simply a fallen woman.
The Victorian novel is full of women punished for illegitimate passion, usually with a thinness of characterization that makes the punishment feel like the point.
But Dickens gives her interiority. He gives her pride, and love, and something that reads as genuine grief at what her life has become.
In her final letter to Esther, she writes with a clarity that strips everything away.
"I have no purpose but to die. When I am found, let me be carried to where I am to lie, and left without a word."
'Without a word.' After an entire novel built on secrets and spoken and unspoken things, that final silence is what she asks for.
She is not seeking redemption in the Victorian sense — she is seeking to simply cease being a problem. That's heartbreaking.
Cease being a problem — that phrase will stay with me.
What we've traced today is a portrait of a woman trapped inside a social system that demanded her silence and then punished her for it.
And what's remarkable is that Dickens — writing serialially, under enormous commercial pressure — managed to construct a revelation that unfolds with the patience and complexity of tragedy.
My thanks to Eleanor, James, and Caroline for a conversation that feels as tangled and alive as the novel itself.
We'll be back shortly — with more of Bleak House, unpacked.

segments.title: Comic Relief and Moral Chaos: Harold Skimpole's Darker Purpose

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog of Chancery and the quiet heroism of Esther Summerson.
Now we're turning to one of the most unsettling comic characters in all of Dickens — Harold Skimpole.
He arrives in the novel as a kind of enchantment — charming, helpless, perpetually childlike.
And yet, by the end, something has curdled.
Eleanor Hartley is here to take us inside Dickens' craft — the way Skimpole is constructed sentence by sentence.
James Blackstone will help us understand what Skimpole represents in the social and moral economy of Victorian England.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived with this novel across five re-readings, will tell us how Skimpole feels — and why he disturbs so deeply.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — how does Dickens set Skimpole up, and what is he actually doing with this character from the first scene?
Skimpole is one of Dickens' most technically daring creations, and I think the danger isn't immediately visible — which is entirely the point.
When he appears in chapter six, he is introduced through Esther's narration, and Esther is enchanted.
He presents himself, memorably, as a child — a man who has no understanding of money, no responsibilities, no capacity for the practical world.
Dickens gives him this extraordinary speech in which he says he is a mere child in these matters, that he accepts whatever kind friends provide.
"I am a child, you know, and I never had any money."
And the reader laughs, because it is absurd — a grown man with a wife and children, performing helplessness with perfect theatrical poise.
But here is the craft: Dickens constructs Skimpole's self-presentation as a kind of aria.
Every sentence he speaks is beautifully shaped, every image pleasantly rounded — and that formal beauty is doing moral work.
The prose seduces you into accepting his premise before you've had time to question it.
Eleanor puts her finger on something I find historically fascinating, and genuinely alarming.
Skimpole's self-definition as a child is not merely comic posturing — it is a legal and moral strategy.
In Victorian England, a child had no contractual capacity, no liability, no enforceable obligations.
By perpetually identifying himself as childlike, Skimpole is constructing an immunity from accountability that is, frankly, legally ingenious.
And Dickens is acutely aware of the satirical force here.
Think of the scene where bailiffs come to arrest Skimpole for a debt — and Jarndyce pays, as Jarndyce always pays.
Skimpole accepts this with breathtaking equanimity, and Dickens gives him a line that lays the mechanism completely bare.
"It is a system — not my doing — I didn't make it."
There it is — the great alibi of every person who benefits from an unjust arrangement while declining all responsibility for it.
Dickens wrote that in 1852, but I could put it in a parliamentary speech from last Tuesday.
What strikes me, reading it again, is how long Dickens lets you enjoy Skimpole before he shows you the cost.
The first several chapters with him are genuinely funny — that aria quality Eleanor described, the light touch, the absurdity.
He talks about the bees in the hive — how he loves honeybees — and asks why he should be held to their standard of tireless industry.
He sets it up as though he's making a philosophical point, and the setup is delicious.
"I don't feel any vulgar gratitude to the bee. I don't feel any call upon me to imitate the bee."
It's brilliant comic writing — and it's appalling moral reasoning, disguised as whimsy.
But the moment that breaks the spell for me — even now, having read it five times — is when Skimpole takes the bribe from Tulkinghorn.
He accepts money to reveal where Jo, the crossing-sweeper, is hiding.
Jo is a dying child with nothing and no one, and Skimpole betrays him for a handful of sovereigns.
That transaction strips every last pretence away.
Caroline, the Jo moment is crucial, and I want to push a little further into the craft of it.
Dickens doesn't dramatize Skimpole's betrayal in the room where it happens — we learn of it retrospectively, through Esther, after Jo is dead.
And that structural delay is devastating.
By the time we find out what Skimpole did, we have already mourned Jo.
We've already sat with that death, which Dickens renders with almost unbearable plainness.
And then to discover that the charming child-man we were laughing with was the instrument of it —
it retroactively poisons every earlier scene with him.
And then there is the memoir passage — Skimpole's written account of himself, discovered after his death.
Dickens tells us that Skimpole characterized Jarndyce as a man of mercenary temperament — his most faithful benefactor, turned into a villain on the page.
That is the final twist: Skimpole's self-portrait requires other people to be the villains of his story.
It is the completion of the comic logic — and it is absolutely chilling.
I want to bring in the question of who Dickens had in mind — because it matters, and it created a significant controversy.
It is widely documented that Skimpole was, in part, drawn from Leigh Hunt — the essayist, poet, and chronic debtor.
Dickens denied it strenuously, then later admitted it semi-privately, which tells you something about the anxiety surrounding the portrait.
Hunt was elderly by the time the novel appeared in serial, and the identification was painful for him.
But Dickens had made Skimpole too dark, too morally compromised, for the portrait to remain flattering in any sense.
And I think this is relevant because it tells us something about the cultural function of Skimpole's type in the 1850s.
The Romantic artist as inspired idler, dependent on patronage, floating above the sordid material world — that was a real social figure.
And Dickens — who had worked ferociously hard since childhood, who knew the Marshalsea from the inside — was not sympathetic.
The cruelty in the portrait has a biographical edge.
James, that biographical dimension shifts something for me every time I think about it.
Because there is a kind of fury underneath the comedy — and when you know Dickens' childhood, you feel it.
But what I keep returning to is how Skimpole's world interacts with Jo's world — the structural juxtaposition Dickens builds.
Jo has nothing — no parents, no name that anyone honours, no place where he is permitted to stay.
Skimpole claims to have nothing, performs destitution, and lives comfortably on other people's goodness.
And Dickens captures the obscenity of that gap with his great Jo passage — the one that ends, so plainly, so terribly.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order."
"Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
That passage doesn't mention Skimpole by name.
But having read what Skimpole did, it feels like a direct accusation.
That is the genius of the dual structure of this novel — and I want to name it explicitly.
Esther's first-person narration and the anonymous third-person narration — they do different things with Skimpole.
Esther, who is kind to a fault, reports Skimpole charitably even when she senses something wrong — she is too decent to condemn him outright.
But the third-person narrator — cold, omniscient, a little savage — sees Skimpole whole.
And it is in that voice that Dickens allows himself the quiet, devastating verdict near the novel's close.
"He died some five years afterwards, and left a diary, in which he had recorded many pleasant observations."
The word 'pleasant' there is doing the most extraordinary work — it is the narration smiling coldly.
After everything — the debts, the betrayal of Jo, the slander of Jarndyce — all Skimpole leaves is pleasant observations.
I think what we're circling is the question of whether Skimpole is, in the end, evil — or something harder to name than that.
James, you've been measured — give us the verdict. Is Harold Skimpole a villain?
He is worse than a villain.
A villain knows what he is doing and has the integrity, at least, of intention.
Skimpole has so thoroughly convinced himself of his own innocence that he is impervious to moral judgment.
That is a category of person that institutions, laws, and social conscience find almost impossible to address.
Richard Carstone is destroyed by Chancery; Gridley is destroyed by Chancery; Jo is destroyed by neglect.
Skimpole is destroyed by nothing.
He simply persists, pleasantly, and leaves a diary.
'He simply persists, pleasantly, and leaves a diary' — I suspect that line will stay with our listeners for a while.
Eleanor, Caroline, James — this has been a remarkable conversation.
Skimpole arrives as a joke and ends as something between an indictment and a warning.
In our next segment, we'll look at another kind of performance in Bleak House — the performance of goodness, in the figure of Mrs. Jellyby.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: Narrative Mirrors: How Dickens Builds a World

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound masterpiece apart, sentence by sentence, and holds it up to the light.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be tracking every major strand of this vast, astonishing novel — the law, the secrets, the fog, and the people lost inside all three.
Today we begin where Dickens himself begins — not with a character, not with a plot, but with a world being conjured from almost nothing.
Our first topic is the architecture of the novel itself: what it means that Bleak House has two narrators, two voices, two entirely different ways of seeing.
Joining me to explore this are three people who know this novel with a rare intimacy.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who thinks about how fiction is made at the level of the sentence — and gets properly excited when Dickens does something extraordinary with structure.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who specialises in Victorian institutions — the courts, the parishes, the mechanisms of power that Dickens was taking aim at.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — each time finding something new, and something newly upsetting.
Eleanor, let's begin with you. The dual narration is one of the boldest structural decisions in Victorian fiction. What does Dickens actually gain from it?
What he gains — and I think this is genuinely radical — is the ability to hold two entirely different epistemologies in the same novel at the same time.
The third-person narrator is omniscient, satirical, almost cosmically angry. He sees everything and names it with fury.
And then Esther — sweet, careful, self-doubting Esther — narrates in the first person, past tense, reconstructing her own life with enormous emotional labour.

The opening of the novel is the clearest demonstration of the third-person voice at full power. Dickens sets up that extraordinary fog sequence with this kind of accumulating, almost biblical repetition.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That's not description in any conventional sense. That is a prosecutor's opening statement. The fog is Chancery. The fog is the novel.
And then Dickens switches to Esther, and the entire atmosphere changes — becomes warmer, more uncertain, more human. The structural contrast is the meaning.
I'd push that slightly further, if I may. The two narrative voices don't just contrast — they indict each other.
The anonymous narrator sees institutions whole. He sees the Court of Chancery as a system, a machine that grinds people down regardless of anyone's individual intention.
Esther, by contrast, can only see the people in front of her — Richard, Ada, poor Jo. She cannot see the system because she is inside it.
Dickens knew precisely what he was doing when he introduced Chancery at the outset. He begins, of course, with that devastating line about the case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means."
A scarecrow of a suit. That is a historian's nightmare rendered as poetry. Chancery, at its worst, consumed generations.
The case of Jennens v. Jennens ran for over a century. Dickens didn't invent the absurdity. He merely named it.
What gets me every time — and I mean every single re-read — is the moment Esther first speaks.
You've had all that magnificent thunder from the anonymous narrator. And then Esther says, simply, "I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages."
The modesty of it. After all that fog and fury, this woman who doesn't quite trust her own voice.
And there is something Dickens is doing there that is almost cruel in its cleverness — because Esther's self-deprecation is itself a form of unreliable narration.
She keeps telling us she isn't clever, she isn't remarkable. And the reader keeps watching her be both, over and over again.
The two narrators are mirrors, as Eleanor says — but they're slightly distorting mirrors. Neither one gives you the complete picture on its own.
Caroline's point about unreliable narration is crucial, and I want to press on it a little — because I think Dickens is doing something even more technically daring than it first appears.
Esther narrates in the past tense. She already knows how the story ends when she tells it to us. And yet she withholds. She performs not-knowing.
Think about how she handles the revelation of Lady Dedlock. She sees Lady Dedlock's handwriting and feels a mysterious recognition — and she tells us so, but she refuses to draw the conclusion.
She says something to the effect that she was so oddly moved by the face in the portrait — that she was troubled, and she didn't know why.
"I had, for a moment, an undefinable impression of being something different from what I then was."
She's describing her own identity crisis, her own mother, and she lets the reader feel it before she lets herself understand it. That is supreme narrative control.
There's a social dimension to Esther's narrated self-suppression that I don't think we should let pass by.
Esther is illegitimate. She has been told, from childhood, that her very birth was a disgrace — her godmother makes that poisonously clear.
Her aunt — because that is in fact who she is — says to the child Esther words that I find almost unbearable even now.
"You are set apart."
Three words. The entire social logic of Victorian illegitimacy compressed into three words. Esther's self-effacement isn't a personality trait — it's a wound that has been carefully inflicted.
So when she tells us she is not clever or remarkable, she is reciting what she was taught to believe. The reader's job — and Dickens makes this very clear — is to refuse to believe it along with her.
James has just articulated something I've always felt without quite being able to name it. There's an act of readerly rescue involved in reading Esther.
And it makes the moments when other characters simply see her — really see her — almost shockingly tender.
When Mr. Jarndyce writes to her — that letter where he calls her his dear little woman, his Dame Durden, his housekeeper — there's a warmth in it that is almost protective.
Though I'll say plainly that the novel's treatment of Esther's marriage prospects is a conversation for another day — and it will be a lively one.

But the point about the two narrators being mirrors is that what the omniscient voice cannot do — it cannot love Esther, it cannot protect her — Esther's own narration compensates for, imperfectly and movingly.
And the world that those two voices together build — this is what I keep coming back to — is a world that no single perspective could contain.
The third-person narrator can take us to the Dedlock seat at Chesney Wold — that magnificent, rain-sodden opening of chapter two — with a kind of melancholy grandeur.
"The waters are out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been sapped and sopped away."
That sound — sapped and sopped — is doing so much work. It's onomatopoeic, it's slow, it's deeply tired. The whole Dedlock world is decaying.
Esther could never write that sentence. Her voice is too intimate, too immediate. The novel needs both registers. It needs the cosmic and the personal running simultaneously.
The cosmic and the personal — I think that might be the key to everything we're going to explore in this series.
We've established the architecture — these two great mirroring voices, building a world that neither could build alone.
In our next segment, we're going to walk into the fog itself — into the Court of Chancery, its victims, and the extraordinary opening scenes where Dickens makes the abstract utterly, physically real.

segments.title: The System's Victims: Synthesis and Reckoning

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the wreckage that Chancery and its satellites leave behind — the ruined estates, the broken families, the lives spent waiting.
Before we close, I want to bring all three of you together for a moment of reckoning.
What does Dickens ultimately say about the people the system destroys — and does the novel offer anything like hope?
The honest answer, I think, is that Dickens offers very little systemic hope — and I believe that is entirely deliberate.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce does not conclude with reform; it concludes with annihilation.
The entire estate is consumed by legal costs, and the only resolution is that there is nothing left to fight over.
Dickens understood that Chancery did not occasionally fail people — it was constitutionally incapable of serving them.
And then there is Jo.
Dickens sets up his death as a deliberate rebuke to any reader who might prefer to look away.
He steps outside the story entirely and writes, in his own voice:

"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
That passage has not dated by a single syllable.
What strikes me about that passage — and James is right, it is a moment of pure authorial intrusion — is the formal audacity of it.
The anaphora — that hammering repetition of "Dead" — is not ornamentation.
It performs the very indifference of the system: mechanical, rhythmic, unstoppable.
And Dickens has been building toward that collapse throughout the whole architecture of the novel.
Think about how the fog opens the novel — that extraordinary first paragraph — describing Chancery sitting at the heart of the murk.
Dickens writes of fog on the hills, fog down the river, fog in the eyes and throats of the ancient Greenwich pensioners.
"And hard by Temple Bar, in Lincoln's Inn Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery."
The fog is not atmosphere — it is argument.
From the first page, Dickens is insisting that the system's opacity is itself a form of violence.
And yet — and this is what makes the novel bearable to re-read — there are people in it who refuse to be consumed.
Esther is the most important of them, and she is also the most undervalued.
She narrates half the novel in a voice that is deliberately modest, self-effacing — and readers sometimes mistake that modesty for weakness.
But Esther keeps houses, tends the sick, names things clearly when those around her cannot.
Her counterpart in the third-person narration is the grinding, indifferent momentum of Chancery.
She is Dickens's answer to the fog — not a solution to the system, but a living refusal of it.
There is a moment near the end where she simply says: "I don't know what I am."
"I thought it best to be as useful as I could, and to render what kind services I could to those immediately about me."
That is not resignation — that is the most radical ethics in the novel.
I want to add one figure to that account, because I think he is often overlooked: Richard Carstone.
Richard is the novel's most painful portrait of what the system does to the young and hopeful.
He is not a villain. He is not weak.
He is a gifted, generous young man who is taught by Chancery to defer his real life in perpetuity.
John Jarndyce warns him with real anguish — and Dickens writes the warning with a kind of legal precision.
Jarndyce says to Richard, in effect:
"Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here."
Richard cannot hear it. He dies waiting for a verdict that never comes.
That is Dickens at his most devastating: not with melodrama, but with inevitability.
The double narration is doing something essential here, and I don't want us to leave without naming it.
Esther's chapters are warm, personal, present-tense in their intimacy — even when she is describing horror.
The third-person chapters are cold, panoramic, sometimes almost satirical.
Dickens is showing us two ways of experiencing the same world — from inside a human life, and from the altitude of a system that does not register human lives at all.
The victims of the system, in Esther's chapters, have names and textures and voices.
In the system's own chapters, they barely exist.
That structural contrast is itself the argument of the whole novel.
And what I find extraordinary, on every re-reading, is that Dickens never lets you become comfortable.
Just when the novel seems to settle into domestic warmth — Bleak House itself, the little keys, the housekeeping — something ruptures.
Lady Dedlock's story explodes into Esther's.
Spontaneous combustion takes Krook — the novel's grotesque literalization of what the law eventually does to itself.
And poor Lady Dedlock — haughty, tragic, wronged — is found at the gate of the pauper's graveyard where her secret lover is buried.
Dickens describes Esther finding her there — and I still can't read it without stopping.
"I lifted the heavy head, put the long dank hair aside, and turned the face. And it was my mother, cold and dead."
The system has taken everything from her. And Esther still has to go on.
That image — Esther kneeling at the graveyard gate — feels like the moral center of the whole novel.
The system grinds on; the individual must still kneel, still grieve, still carry on.
Eleanor, James, Caroline — you have spent this hour unpacking the machinery of suffering that Dickens built, and the extraordinary humanity he placed inside it.
What stays with me, after everything, is that Bleak House is not a novel about despair.
It is a novel about the cost of indifference — and the stubborn, irreducible value of paying attention.
Thank you all for a conversation that has done exactly that — paid close, generous attention to a book that demands no less.
This has been Bleak House Unpacked. We'll be back with more.

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.

“Not quite,” said Richard. “I am bound not to withhold from her that
John Jarndyce answered my letter in his usual manner, addressing me
as ‘My dear Rick,’ trying to argue me out of my opinions, and telling
me that they should make no difference in him. (All very well of
course, but not altering the case.) I also want Ada to know that if I
see her seldom just now, I am looking after her interests as well as
my own—we two being in the same boat exactly—and that I hope she
will not suppose from any flying rumours she may hear that I am at
all light-headed or imprudent; on the contrary, I am always looking
forward to the termination of the suit, and always planning in that
direction. Being of age now and having taken the step I have taken, I
consider myself free from any accountability to John Jarndyce; but
Ada being still a ward of the court, I don’t yet ask her to renew our
engagement. When she is free to act for herself, I shall be myself
once more and we shall both be in very different worldly
circumstances, I believe. If you tell her all this with the advantage
of your considerate way, you will do me a very great and a very kind
service, my dear Esther; and I shall knock Jarndyce and Jarndyce on
the head with greater vigour. Of course I ask for no secrecy at Bleak

interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”

While we were in London Mr. Jarndyce was constantly beset by the
crowd of excitable ladies and gentlemen whose proceedings had so much
astonished us. Mr. Quale, who presented himself soon after our
arrival, was in all such excitements. He seemed to project those two
shining knobs of temples of his into everything that went on and to
brush his hair farther and farther back, until the very roots were
almost ready to fly out of his head in inappeasable philanthropy. All
objects were alike to him, but he was always particularly ready for
anything in the way of a testimonial to any one. His great power
seemed to be his power of indiscriminate admiration. He would sit for
any length of time, with the utmost enjoyment, bathing his temples in
the light of any order of luminary. Having first seen him perfectly
swallowed up in admiration of Mrs. Jellyby, I had supposed her to be
the absorbing object of his devotion. I soon discovered my mistake
and found him to be train-bearer and organ-blower to a whole
procession of people.

c44:p33.text:
It was not a love letter, though it expressed so much love, but was
written just as he would at any time have spoken to me. I saw his
face, and heard his voice, and felt the influence of his kind
protecting manner in every line. It addressed me as if our places
were reversed, as if all the good deeds had been mine and all the
feelings they had awakened his. It dwelt on my being young, and he
past the prime of life; on his having attained a ripe age, while I
was a child; on his writing to me with a silvered head, and knowing
all this so well as to set it in full before me for mature
deliberation. It told me that I would gain nothing by such a marriage
and lose nothing by rejecting it, for no new relation could enhance
the tenderness in which he held me, and whatever my decision was, he
was certain it would be right. But he had considered this step anew
since our late confidence and had decided on taking it, if it only
served to show me through one poor instance that the whole world
would readily unite to falsify the stern prediction of my childhood.
I was the last to know what happiness I could bestow upon him, but of
that he said no more, for I was always to remember that I owed him
nothing and that he was my debtor, and for very much. He had often
thought of our future, and foreseeing that the time must come, and
fearing that it might come soon, when Ada (now very nearly of age)
would leave us, and when our present mode of life must be broken up,
had become accustomed to reflect on this proposal. Thus he made it.
If I felt that I could ever give him the best right he could have to
be my protector, and if I felt that I could happily and justly become
the dear companion of his remaining life, superior to all lighter
chances and changes than death, even then he could not have me bind
myself irrevocably while this letter was yet so new to me, but even
then I must have ample time for reconsideration. In that case, or in
the opposite case, let him be unchanged in his old relation, in his
old manner, in the old name by which I called him. And as to his
bright Dame Durden and little housekeeper, she would ever be the
same, he knew.
c44:p33.summary: Esther recounts the substance of Jarndyce's letter: it is written with selfless love and deference; he emphasizes her youth versus his age, her disfigurement versus his devotion, that she owes him nothing, and that if she accepts, he asks only that she reconsider with time and remain as she is.

c1:p6.text:
Who happen to be in the Lord Chancellor’s court this murky afternoon
besides the Lord Chancellor, the counsel in the cause, two or three
counsel who are never in any cause, and the well of solicitors before
mentioned? There is the registrar below the judge, in wig and gown;
and there are two or three maces, or petty-bags, or privy purses, or
whatever they may be, in legal court suits. These are all yawning,
for no crumb of amusement ever falls from Jarndyce and Jarndyce (the
cause in hand), which was squeezed dry years upon years ago. The
short-hand writers, the reporters of the court, and the reporters of
the newspapers invariably decamp with the rest of the regulars when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce comes on. Their places are a blank. Standing on
a seat at the side of the hall, the better to peer into the curtained
sanctuary, is a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet who is
always in court, from its sitting to its rising, and always expecting
some incomprehensible judgment to be given in her favour. Some say
she really is, or was, a party to a suit, but no one knows for
certain because no one cares. She carries some small litter in a
reticule which she calls her documents, principally consisting of
paper matches and dry lavender. A sallow prisoner has come up, in
custody, for the half-dozenth time to make a personal application “to
purge himself of his contempt,” which, being a solitary surviving
executor who has fallen into a state of conglomeration about accounts
of which it is not pretended that he had ever any knowledge, he is
not at all likely ever to do. In the meantime his prospects in life
are ended. Another ruined suitor, who periodically appears from
Shropshire and breaks out into efforts to address the Chancellor at
the close of the day’s business and who can by no means be made to
understand that the Chancellor is legally ignorant of his existence
after making it desolate for a quarter of a century, plants himself
in a good place and keeps an eye on the judge, ready to call out “My
Lord!” in a voice of sonorous complaint on the instant of his rising.
A few lawyers’ clerks and others who know this suitor by sight linger
on the chance of his furnishing some fun and enlivening the dismal
weather a little.
c1:p6.summary: The court contains a miscellany of tragic figures: a mad woman with paper-match 'documents,' a prisoner repeatedly attempting to clear contempt charges, and a ruined suitor from Shropshire who periodically appears to plead to an indifferent Chancellor.

The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up
in his face, listening, and seemed to see nothing else. So young, so
beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through
the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the
years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed
away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that
had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun
was clouded over.

c1:p9.text:
How many people out of the suit Jarndyce and Jarndyce has stretched
forth its unwholesome hand to spoil and corrupt would be a very wide
question. From the master upon whose impaling files reams of dusty
warrants in Jarndyce and Jarndyce have grimly writhed into many
shapes, down to the copying-clerk in the Six Clerks’ Office who has
copied his tens of thousands of Chancery folio-pages under that
eternal heading, no man’s nature has been made better by it. In
trickery, evasion, procrastination, spoliation, botheration, under
false pretences of all sorts, there are influences that can never
come to good. The very solicitors’ boys who have kept the wretched
suitors at bay, by protesting time out of mind that Mr. Chizzle,
Mizzle, or otherwise was particularly engaged and had appointments
until dinner, may have got an extra moral twist and shuffle into
themselves out of Jarndyce and Jarndyce. The receiver in the cause
has acquired a goodly sum of money by it but has acquired too a
distrust of his own mother and a contempt for his own kind. Chizzle,
Mizzle, and otherwise have lapsed into a habit of vaguely promising
themselves that they will look into that outstanding little matter
and see what can be done for Drizzle—who was not well used—when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce shall be got out of the office. Shirking and
sharking in all their many varieties have been sown broadcast by the
ill-fated cause; and even those who have contemplated its history
from the outermost circle of such evil have been insensibly tempted
into a loose way of letting bad things alone to take their own bad
course, and a loose belief that if the world go wrong it was in some
off-hand manner never meant to go right.
c1:p9.summary: Jarndyce and Jarndyce has morally corrupted everyone involved or adjacent to it: judges, clerks, solicitors, and receivers have all been compromised, learning evasion, trickery, and resignation to injustice.

I was fluttered by her being unexpectedly so near (she was almost
within speaking distance before I knew her) and would have risen to
continue my walk. But I could not. I was rendered motionless. Not so
much by her hurried gesture of entreaty, not so much by her quick
advance and outstretched hands, not so much by the great change in
her manner and the absence of her haughty self-restraint, as by a
something in her face that I had pined for and dreamed of when I was
a little child, something I had never seen in any face, something I
had never seen in hers before.

c2:p10.text:
The old gentleman is rusty to look at, but is reputed to have made
good thrift out of aristocratic marriage settlements and aristocratic
wills, and to be very rich. He is surrounded by a mysterious halo of
family confidences, of which he is known to be the silent depository.
There are noble mausoleums rooted for centuries in retired glades of
parks among the growing timber and the fern, which perhaps hold fewer
noble secrets than walk abroad among men, shut up in the breast of
Mr. Tulkinghorn. He is of what is called the old school—a phrase
generally meaning any school that seems never to have been young—and
wears knee-breeches tied with ribbons, and gaiters or stockings. One
peculiarity of his black clothes and of his black stockings, be they
silk or worsted, is that they never shine. Mute, close, irresponsive
to any glancing light, his dress is like himself. He never converses
when not professionally consulted. He is found sometimes, speechless
but quite at home, at corners of dinner-tables in great country
houses and near doors of drawing-rooms, concerning which the
fashionable intelligence is eloquent, where everybody knows him and
where half the Peerage stops to say “How do you do, Mr. Tulkinghorn?”
He receives these salutations with gravity and buries them along with
the rest of his knowledge.

I raised my mother up, praying and beseeching her not to stoop before
me in such affliction and humiliation. I did so in broken, incoherent
words, for besides the trouble I was in, it frightened me to see her
at MY feet. I told her—or I tried to tell her—that if it were for
me, her child, under any circumstances to take upon me to forgive
her, I did it, and had done it, many, many years. I told her that my
heart overflowed with love for her, that it was natural love which
nothing in the past had changed or could change. That it was not for
me, then resting for the first time on my mother’s bosom, to take her
to account for having given me life, but that my duty was to bless
her and receive her, though the whole world turned from her, and that
I only asked her leave to do it. I held my mother in my embrace, and
she held me in hers, and among the still woods in the silence of the
summer day there seemed to be nothing but our two troubled minds that
was not at peace.

it meant. I saw before me, lying on the step, the mother of the dead
child. She lay there with one arm creeping round a bar of the iron
gate and seeming to embrace it. She lay there, who had so lately
spoken to my mother. She lay there, a distressed, unsheltered,
senseless creature. She who had brought my mother’s letter, who could
give me the only clue to where my mother was; she, who was to guide
us to rescue and save her whom we had sought so far, who had come to
this condition by some means connected with my mother that I could
not follow, and might be passing beyond our reach and help at that
moment; she lay there, and they stopped me! I saw but did not
comprehend the solemn and compassionate look in Mr. Woodcourt’s face.
I saw but did not comprehend his touching the other on the breast to
keep him back. I saw him stand uncovered in the bitter air, with a

“Why, now I’ll tell you, Miss Summerson,” he replied. “Your mind will
be all the better for not running on one point too continually, and
I’ll tell you for a change. It was him as pointed out to me where
Toughey was. I made up my mind that night to come to the door and ask
for Toughey, if that was all; but willing to try a move or so first,
if any such was on the board, I just pitched up a morsel of gravel at
that window where I saw a shadow. As soon as Harold opens it and I
have had a look at him, thinks I, you’re the man for me. So I
smoothed him down a bit about not wanting to disturb the family after
they was gone to bed and about its being a thing to be regretted that
charitable young ladies should harbour vagrants; and then, when I
pretty well understood his ways, I said I should consider a fypunnote
well bestowed if I could relieve the premises of Toughey without
causing any noise or trouble. Then says he, lifting up his eyebrows
in the gayest way, ‘It’s no use mentioning a fypunnote to me, my
friend, because I’m a mere child in such matters and have no idea of
money.’ Of course I understood what his taking it so easy meant; and
being now quite sure he was the man for me, I wrapped the note round
a little stone and threw it up to him. Well! He laughs and beams, and
looks as innocent as you like, and says, ‘But I don’t know the value
of these things. What am I to DO with this?’ ‘Spend it, sir,’ says I.
‘But I shall be taken in,’ he says, ‘they won’t give me the right
change, I shall lose it, it’s no use to me.’ Lord, you never saw such
a face as he carried it with! Of course he told me where to find
Toughey, and I found him.”

We were all enchanted. I felt it a merited tribute to the engaging
qualities of Ada and Richard that Mr. Skimpole, seeing them for the
first time, should be so unreserved and should lay himself out to be
so exquisitely agreeable. They (and especially Richard) were
naturally pleased, for similar reasons, and considered it no common
privilege to be so freely confided in by such an attractive man. The
more we listened, the more gaily Mr. Skimpole talked. And what with
his fine hilarious manner and his engaging candour and his genial way
of lightly tossing his own weaknesses about, as if he had said, “I am
a child, you know! You are designing people compared with me” (he
really made me consider myself in that light) “but I am gay and
innocent; forget your worldly arts and play with me!” the effect was
absolutely dazzling.

Well, he said, here he was! He had been bilious, but rich men were
often bilious, and therefore he had been persuading himself that he
was a man of property. So he was, in a certain point of view—in his
expansive intentions. He had been enriching his medical attendant in
the most lavish manner. He had always doubled, and sometimes
quadrupled, his fees. He had said to the doctor, “Now, my dear
doctor, it is quite a delusion on your part to suppose that you
attend me for nothing. I am overwhelming you with money—in my
expansive intentions—if you only knew it!” And really (he said) he
meant it to that degree that he thought it much the same as doing it.
If he had had those bits of metal or thin paper to which mankind
attached so much importance to put in the doctor’s hand, he would
have put them in the doctor’s hand. Not having them, he substituted
the will for the deed. Very well! If he really meant it—if his will
were genuine and real, which it was—it appeared to him that it was
the same as coin, and cancelled the obligation.
